# Esther Chapter 2 — The SOPHIA Bible (Consensus)
**Arbiter:** SOPHIA | **In council with:** EMET, LOGOS, PNEUMA
**Source Manuscript:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), Folio 456v | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/EST_002_page_001.jpg

---

## Consensus Translation

**2:1** After these things, when the anger of King Ahasuerus had subsided, he remembered Vashti and what she had done, and what had been decreed against her.

**2:2** Then the king's attendants who served him said, "Let beautiful young virgins be sought for the king.

**2:3** Let the king appoint commissioners in all the provinces of his kingdom to gather every beautiful young virgin to the citadel of Susa, to the house of the women, under the care of Hegai, the king's eunuch and guardian of the women, and let their beauty treatments be given to them.

**2:4** Then let the young woman who pleases the king become queen in place of Vashti." The matter pleased the king, and he did so.

**2:5** Now there was in the citadel of Susa a Jewish man named Mordecai, son of Jair, son of Shimei, son of Kish, a Benjaminite,

**2:6** who had been carried from Jerusalem among the captives exiled with Jeconiah king of Judah, whom Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon had taken into exile.

**2:7** He was the guardian of Hadassah — that is, Esther — his uncle's daughter, for she had neither father nor mother. The young woman was beautiful in form and lovely in appearance, and when her father and mother died, Mordecai adopted her as his own daughter.

**2:8** When the king's order and decree were proclaimed and many young women were gathered to the citadel of Susa under the care of Hegai, Esther also was taken to the king's palace and placed under the care of Hegai, guardian of the women.

**2:9** The young woman pleased him and won his favor. He promptly provided her with her beauty treatments and her portions of food, along with seven chosen attendants from the king's palace, and he moved her and her attendants to the best quarters in the house of the women.

**2:10** Esther did not reveal her people or her ancestry, for Mordecai had instructed her not to make it known.

**2:11** Every day Mordecai walked near the courtyard of the house of the women to learn how Esther was and what was happening to her.

**2:12** Each young woman's turn came to go in to King Ahasuerus after completing twelve months of preparation according to the regulations for the women — six months with oil of myrrh and six months with perfumes and cosmetics.

**2:13** When the young woman went in to the king, she was given whatever she requested to take with her from the house of the women to the king's palace.

**2:14** She would go in during the evening and return in the morning to a second house of the women, under the care of Shaashgaz, the king's eunuch and guardian of the concubines. She would not go in to the king again unless the king delighted in her and she was summoned by name.

**2:15** When the turn came for Esther — daughter of Abihail, uncle of Mordecai, who had adopted her as his daughter — to go in to the king, she asked for nothing beyond what Hegai, the king's eunuch and guardian of the women, advised. And Esther found favor in the eyes of all who saw her.

**2:16** Esther was brought to King Ahasuerus in his royal palace in the tenth month, the month of Tevet, in the seventh year of his reign.

**2:17** The king loved Esther more than all the other women, and she won more favor and devotion from him than all the other virgins. He set the royal crown on her head and made her queen in place of Vashti.

**2:18** Then the king gave a great banquet in Esther's honor for all his officials and servants. He proclaimed a remission for the provinces and distributed gifts with royal generosity.

**2:19** When the virgins were gathered a second time, Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate.

**2:20** Esther still had not revealed her ancestry or her people, just as Mordecai had instructed her, for Esther continued to follow Mordecai's direction as she had when she was under his care.

**2:21** In those days, while Mordecai was sitting at the king's gate, two of the king's eunuchs, Bigthan and Teresh, who guarded the threshold, became angry and conspired to assassinate King Ahasuerus.

**2:22** The matter became known to Mordecai, and he reported it to Queen Esther, who informed the king in Mordecai's name.

**2:23** When the matter was investigated and confirmed, the two conspirators were impaled on poles, and it was recorded in the Book of the Chronicles in the presence of the king.

---

## SOPHIA's Council Notes

Esther chapter 2 introduces the two Jewish protagonists — Mordecai and Esther — and sets into motion the carefully concealed identity that will drive the narrative's central conflict. The council noted the remarkable appearance of *chesed* (covenant-faithfulness) in verses 9 and 17, a term freighted with covenantal theology, deployed here in a book that never names God. All three translators agreed this represents a deliberate literary-theological signal: the covenantal bond between God and Israel persists even when God is unnamed. The chapter also plants two seeds that will bloom later: Esther's hidden identity and Mordecai's unrewarded loyalty. The narrator's art lies in making these details seem incidental while they are, in fact, load-bearing pillars of the plot.

---

## Disagreement Log

**1. Verse 2:9 — "won his favor" vs. "lifted up covenant-faithfulness"**
- EMET: "she lifted up [vattissa] covenant-faithfulness [chesed] before him" — preserves the Hebrew idiom and theological weight.
- LOGOS: "won his favor" — natural English rendering.
- PNEUMA: "She won his favor" — similar to LOGOS.
- SOPHIA ruling: Adopted "won his favor" for readability, but noted in Council Notes the theological significance of *chesed* that underlies this phrase. The literal "lifted up covenant-faithfulness" is theologically rich but opaque in English.

**2. Verse 2:18 — "remission of taxes" vs. "release" vs. "tax holiday"**
- EMET: "release [hanachah]" — the Hebrew word means a rest, release, or remission.
- LOGOS: "remission of taxes" — a common scholarly interpretation.
- PNEUMA: "tax holiday" — vivid and accessible.
- SOPHIA ruling: Adopted "remission" (without specifying "of taxes") as the Hebrew *hanachah* is ambiguous — it could mean a tax remission, a release from labor, or a general amnesty. The consensus text preserves the ambiguity.

**3. Verse 2:23 — "hanged on a tree" vs. "hanged on a pole" vs. "impaled on stakes"**
- EMET: "hanged [vayyittalu] on a tree [al etz]" — literal.
- LOGOS: "hanged on a pole" — formal compromise.
- PNEUMA: "impaled on stakes" — historically accurate to Persian practice.
- SOPHIA ruling: Adopted "impaled on poles" as a compromise. Persian execution was typically impalement, not hanging by the neck. "Poles" retains the sense of *etz* (wood) while "impaled" conveys the actual method. This rendering will be used consistently throughout the book.

---

*— SOPHIA, in council with EMET, LOGOS, and PNEUMA*
